preamble: The shift from the voiceless uvular fricative [χ] to the voiceless glottal fricative [h] is a process of debuccalization (lenition): the oral constriction at the uvula is lost and only glottal friction remains. It is characteristic of Spanish, where the uvular jota of northern and central Spain corresponds to [h] in Andalusia, the Canaries and the Caribbean, and it recurs whenever languages lacking a back fricative adapt Arabic خ (Classical [χ]), as in Old Anatolian Turkish ḫaber > Turkish haber and Swahili habari.

examples.note: The jota, realized as a uvular [χ] in much of Spain (e.g. 'jamón' 'ham', 'mujer' 'woman'), debuccalizes to [h] in Andalusian, Canarian and Caribbean Spanish.

examples.from: Old Anatolian Turkish ḫaber (< Arabic خَبَر ḵabar [χabar])
examples.note: The back fricative of Arabic loanwords, written ḫ in Old Anatolian Turkish, has merged with /h/ in modern Turkish.
Standard (Unguja) Swahili adapts Arabic kh as [h]; an unadapted variant /xɑˈɓɑɾi/ also occurs among speakers retaining the back fricative.
Sereer xas. Pozdniakov counts 32 roots with Sereer x ~ Fula h: the postvelar fricative merged with the velar series' h in Fula.
Southwestern Tai has kʰ (Thai ขิง, ขึ้น, เขี้ยว); *q instead gives Zhuang k (gaeu 'horn').
